questions.stem: Athens' nearest neighbours shaped Pericles' policies. Which pairing of a neighbour and its relationship with Athens is correct?
options: Boeotia - an island state that supplied Athens with most of its timber
Aegina - a mountain state on the border of Attica that bred the cavalry
Corinth - a city on Euboea that Athens settled with its own cleruchs in the 440s BCE
Megara - a small state on the isthmus whose ports and loyalty mattered to Athens
questions.explanation: Megara controlled routes across the isthmus and had ports on both gulfs, so its alliance or hostility mattered to Athens. Boeotia lay north of Attica on land, Aegina was an island rival in the Saronic Gulf, and Corinth stood at the isthmus.

questions.stem: Which reformer is usually credited with founding Athenian democracy in 508/7 BCE by reorganising the citizens into ten tribes?
options: Solon
Ephialtes
Pisistratus
Cleisthenes
questions.explanation: Cleisthenes created the ten tribes and the council of 500. He was also Pericles' great-uncle, a link to the Alcmaeonid family that mattered to Pericles' career.

questions.stem: How did the reforms of Ephialtes in 462/1 BCE prepare the ground for Pericles' democracy?
options: They abolished the election of generals and chose all officials by lot
They gave the vote in the assembly to metics and to citizen women
They ended the use of ostracism and restored the old judicial powers of the archons
They moved power from the Areopagus to the council, assembly and courts
questions.explanation: Ephialtes stripped the aristocratic Areopagus of most of its powers, leaving it homicide trials, and passed them to popular bodies. Pericles was his associate and, after Ephialtes was murdered, became the leading figure of the democrats.

questions.stem: Pericles' father Xanthippus was:
options: a metic from Miletus who was granted citizenship for bravery at Salamis
an Athenian commander at the battle of Mycale in 479 BCE
a Spartan king who married into an Athenian family
the tyrant of Athens expelled by Cleisthenes in 510 BCE
questions.explanation: Xanthippus was ostracised in the 480s, recalled during the Persian invasion and commanded the Athenians at Mycale. Pericles' mother Agariste belonged to the Alcmaeonid family.

questions.stem: Pericles' mother came from the Alcmaeonid family. How could this help and hinder him?
options: It made him a metic, so he could never hold office in Athens
It linked him to Cleisthenes, but the family carried an old curse that enemies used
It made him heir to the throne of Sparta, which Athenians feared
It gave him automatic membership of the board of ten generals for the rest of his life
questions.explanation: The Alcmaeonids were famous for Cleisthenes but also bore an ancestral curse for sacrilege. Thucydides says that before the war the Spartans demanded that Athens expel those under the curse, aiming at Pericles.

questions.stem: Plutarch names the philosopher Anaxagoras as the teacher who most influenced Pericles. What did Plutarch believe Pericles gained from him?
options: Training in hoplite tactics and the command of armies on land
Skill in Egyptian astronomy, which he used to reform the calendar
Knowledge of Spartan law and custom, which he later used to draft his citizenship law
A rational outlook, a lofty manner of speaking and calm in the face of events
questions.explanation: Plutarch says Anaxagoras gave Pericles a dignified style and freedom from superstition, illustrated by stories of natural explanations for omens. Damon, his teacher in music, was also said to advise him politically.

questions.stem: In 472 BCE the young Pericles served as choregos, paying for the chorus of which play?
options: Aristophanes' Acharnians
Aeschylus's Persians
Sophocles' Antigone
Euripides' Medea
questions.explanation: A record of dramatic victories names Pericles as choregos for Aeschylus's Persians, which celebrated Salamis. Antigone, Medea and Acharnians all came decades later.

questions.stem: In 463 BCE Pericles was one of the prosecutors of Cimon, who was accused of taking bribes not to attack Macedon. What does this episode show about Pericles' early career?
options: He was Cimon's closest ally and spoke in his defence
He was already sole ruler of Athens and judged the case himself
He had been ostracised and prosecuted Cimon by sending a letter from abroad
He was emerging as an opponent of Cimon, the leading conservative
questions.explanation: Cimon was acquitted, and Plutarch says Pericles' part was mild, but the case placed him on the side of Ephialtes against Cimon. Cimon was ostracised soon after.

questions.stem: According to the Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians, why did Pericles introduce pay for jurors?
options: To reduce the number of jurors, since only men who were paid by the state could serve
To counter Cimon, who won support by using his private wealth for the people
To reward the hoplites who had fought at Marathon and their sons
To force metics to serve as jurors in place of busy citizens
questions.explanation: The source says Pericles, lacking Cimon's fortune, gave the people their own money through state pay. Paying jurors allowed poorer citizens to serve on the courts.

questions.stem: Pericles' law of 451/0 BCE limited Athenian citizenship to:
options: landowners in one of the two richest property classes
those who had lived in Attica for at least ten years
those with an Athenian father and an Athenian mother
men whose fathers had served in the Persian Wars
questions.explanation: The citizenship law required both parents to be Athenian. Its motives are debated: it limited who shared in the benefits of citizenship, at a time when those benefits were growing.

questions.stem: Pericles introduced state pay for public service, and limited citizenship to those with two Athenian parents. Which judgement best links these two measures?
options: Both measures were designed to weaken the thetes in the assembly
The two measures contradicted each other and were both repealed within a few years
Citizenship now brought real rewards, so who counted as a citizen mattered more
Both measures aimed to give metics a larger share in government
questions.explanation: Pay for jurors and others made citizenship valuable, and the citizenship law restricted that privilege. Many historians read them together as democratic for citizens but exclusive towards outsiders.

questions.stem: The architects of the Parthenon were:
options: Ictinus and Callicrates
Mnesicles and Phidias
Hippodamus and Damon
Myron and Polykleitos
questions.explanation: Ictinus and Callicrates designed the Parthenon, begun in 447 BCE, with Phidias overseeing its sculpture. Mnesicles designed the Propylaea, and Hippodamus planned the Piraeus.

questions.stem: Plutarch says Pericles' opponents complained that Athens was decking itself out like a vain woman with jewels bought from the allies' money. How did Pericles reply, according to Plutarch?
options: The buildings were temporary and would be sold to repay the allies
Athens owed the allies no account while it protected them from Persia
The money came only from Athenian silver and not from the allies at all
The allies had asked for the buildings and voted to pay for them
questions.explanation: In Plutarch's account Pericles argued that the allies paid for protection, which Athens gave, so surplus funds could be spent on the city. The exchange shows how the building program was tied to the empire.

questions.stem: Plutarch says the building program gave work and wages to many trades: stone-cutters, carpenters, metal-workers, carriers and others. Which purpose does this point to?
options: Training young soldiers for war by making them haul the stone
Paying the allies back for the tribute they had sent
Reducing the number of slaves held by rich families
Spreading the profits of empire among ordinary citizens
questions.explanation: Plutarch presents the program as a way to employ those who did not serve in the army or fleet. Other aims included honouring the gods and displaying Athenian power.

questions.stem: When the assembly criticised the cost of the buildings, Plutarch says Pericles offered to pay himself, if the buildings carried his name rather than the city's. The people told him to spend public money freely. What does the story suggest about his leadership?
options: He was the sole owner of the buildings and could rename them at will
He had no influence in the assembly and was always outvoted
He paid for the whole program from his own estate in the end
He used his standing with the demos to win support for his own policies
questions.explanation: Whether or not the story is exact, Plutarch uses it to show Pericles turning criticism into a vote of confidence. It fits his method of leading the assembly through persuasion and prestige.

questions.stem: Pericles' power rested legally on:
options: his position as high priest of Athena Polias
a special office of dictator voted in wartime
repeated election as one of the ten generals
a lifetime appointment as eponymous archon
questions.explanation: Pericles held no permanent office: he was elected strategos year after year and led through his speeches in the assembly. Plutarch says he held the generalship continuously for at least fifteen years.

questions.stem: In about 443 BCE Pericles' main rival, Thucydides son of Melesias, was ostracised. Why was this a turning point?
options: It forced Pericles into exile as well, since ostracism removed both of the rivals
It removed the leader of organised opposition, leaving Pericles dominant
It ended the Delian League, since Thucydides had been its treasurer
It made Pericles king of Athens with power to pass laws alone
questions.explanation: Thucydides son of Melesias, not the historian, led the critics of the building program. His ostracism left Pericles without a serious rival for over a decade.

questions.stem: Comic poets nicknamed Pericles 'the Olympian', and Plutarch says he kept away from dinner parties and social gatherings. What do these details suggest about his methods?
options: He won support mainly by hosting lavish feasts for the poor
He cultivated dignity and distance so that his rare speeches carried weight
He avoided politics altogether and left decisions to his friends
He ruled by fear, using a personal bodyguard of armed Scythian archers at all times
questions.explanation: Pericles kept a reserved public image and saved his own speeches for important matters, using associates for routine business. This set him apart from rivals such as Cimon, who used open-handed generosity.

questions.stem: Thucydides says Pericles was clearly incorruptible and that he led the people rather than being led by them. Which conclusion is best supported by this judgement?
options: He let the assembly decide all policy, following whatever it wanted
His influence rested on trust in his honesty and his ability to restrain the demos
He held absolute legal power, so the assembly could not oppose him
He was unpopular, and kept office only because elections were rigged
questions.explanation: Thucydides contrasts Pericles with later leaders who flattered the people. His authority came from reputation and persuasion, not from any office above the law, and he could still be fined and deposed.

questions.stem: Plutarch says Pericles proposed a congress of all Greeks at Athens to discuss rebuilding the temples burned by the Persians and keeping the seas safe. What happened?
options: All the Greek states attended and made Athens their leader
Persia paid for the temples, ending the need for the league
The congress met at Delphi and voted to dissolve the league
Sparta opposed it, and the congress never met
questions.explanation: Plutarch reports that Spartan opposition blocked the Congress Decree. It shows Pericles presenting Athens as leader of the Greeks, though some scholars doubt the decree's authenticity.

questions.stem: Pericles sent Athenian settlers to places such as the Thracian Chersonese. How did these cleruchies serve his imperial policy?
options: They returned land to allies who had lost it in the Persian Wars
They moved Athenian slaves out of Attica to reduce the risk of revolt
They were trading posts run by metics, which paid tax to Sparta
They gave land to poorer Athenians and placed loyal garrisons among the allies
questions.explanation: Cleruchs remained citizens and guarded strategic areas such as the route to the Black Sea, while relieving poverty at home. The allies who lost land resented them.

questions.stem: When Samos revolted in 440 BCE, Pericles led the Athenian response. What was the outcome?
options: After a long siege Samos surrendered, pulled down its walls and gave up its fleet
Samos defeated the Athenian fleet and became leader of a rival league
Pericles negotiated a peace that let Samos leave the league freely
Persia occupied Samos, and Athens abandoned its allies in the eastern Aegean for good
questions.explanation: Thucydides says Samos surrendered in the ninth month of the siege, demolishing its walls, handing over its ships and paying costs. The revolt showed Pericles' determination to hold the empire by force.

questions.stem: In 446 BCE Euboea and Megara revolted and a Spartan army invaded Attica. Pericles crushed Euboea and then agreed the Thirty Years Peace. What does this suggest about his imperial policy?
options: He accepted limits on land power to secure Athens' control of its sea empire
He planned to conquer the Peloponnese and end Sparta as a power
He gave up the empire to win peace with Sparta at any price
He placed Athens and its allies under Spartan protection
questions.explanation: Athens lost its mainland holdings but kept Euboea and its maritime empire, which Pericles treated as the core of Athenian power. He later warned the Athenians not to try to extend the empire during the war.

questions.stem: In the 'Golden Age' of Periclean Athens, the historian who lived in Athens and wrote of the Persian Wars was:
options: Polybius
Plutarch
Herodotus
Xenophon
questions.explanation: Herodotus spent time in Athens during Pericles' ascendancy. Xenophon wrote in the fourth century, and Polybius and Plutarch much later.

questions.stem: Aspasia, Pericles' partner in later life, came from:
options: Thebes
Miletus
Sparta
Corinth
questions.explanation: Aspasia was a Milesian and so, in Athens, a metic. Because of Pericles' own citizenship law, their son could not be a citizen without a special grant.

questions.stem: After Pericles' two legitimate sons died in the plague, the Athenians granted citizenship to his son by Aspasia. Why was this notable?
options: It reversed the ostracism that had been passed on Pericles
It made an exception to the citizenship law Pericles himself had proposed
It was the first time any Athenian woman had been made a citizen
It made the boy king of Athens in place of his father
questions.explanation: Under Pericles' law of 451/0 a son of a foreign mother was not a citizen. Plutarch presents the grant as the people's pity for Pericles' losses.

questions.stem: Before the war, Plutarch says Pericles' enemies attacked him through his associates: Phidias, Anaxagoras and Aspasia. What was their likely aim?
options: To stop the building program, which had not yet begun
To damage Pericles' reputation without facing him directly
To win the friendship of Sparta by punishing Athenian artists
To raise money for the war from their confiscated property
questions.explanation: Phidias was accused over the Athena Parthenos, and Anaxagoras and Aspasia faced charges linked to impiety. Plutarch sees the prosecutions as attacks on Pericles himself, since he was too strong to attack openly.

questions.stem: Thucydides says that by Pericles' advice the Athenians brought their families and goods in from the countryside when the Spartans invaded. What was the purpose?
options: To avoid a land battle against the stronger Spartan army and rely on the fleet
To lure the Spartans into Attica and defeat them in a single hoplite battle
To allow the Spartans to occupy Athens while the Athenians fled to Salamis
To prepare the countryside for a joint defence with Spartan allies
questions.explanation: Pericles' plan was to accept the ravaging of Attica, keep the people behind the walls, use naval raids and keep the allies under control. He believed Athens' sea power and revenue would outlast Sparta.

questions.stem: When the Spartans ravaged Acharnae in 431 BCE, many Athenians demanded to march out. Thucydides says Pericles did not call an assembly or meeting. Why?
options: The law forbade any assembly to meet while an enemy army was inside the borders of Attica
He had already agreed a truce with Archidamus in secret
He feared an angry vote would force a battle his strategy aimed to avoid
He was away commanding the fleet, so the assembly could not meet
questions.explanation: Pericles judged that a meeting held in anger might vote for a pitched battle, so he used his authority as general to keep the citizens inside. It shows both his control and the strain his strategy placed on Athenians.

questions.stem: Some modern historians argue that Pericles' defensive strategy was flawed. Which argument would they most likely make?
options: It risked everything on one great land battle against Spartan hoplites
It left the Athenian fleet idle and gave Sparta control of the sea
It required alliances with Persia that Athens could not obtain
It could not force Sparta to make peace and depended on Athenian patience
questions.explanation: Critics say the strategy aimed to wear Sparta down without a way to win decisively, and it relied on morale that the plague then shattered. Defenders point to Thucydides' view that later leaders lost by abandoning it.

questions.stem: During the plague, the Athenians turned against Pericles. What happened to him in 430 BCE?
options: He resigned and handed his command to Cleon for life
He was fined and removed as general, but soon re-elected
He was ostracised and spent ten years in exile in Sparta
He was put to death by the assembly for causing the plague
questions.explanation: Thucydides says the Athenians fined him, then soon elected him general again and entrusted affairs to him. He died of the plague in 429 BCE.

questions.stem: Thucydides argues that after Pericles' death his successors, competing for leadership, pandered to the people and abandoned his advice. Which later event does Thucydides treat as the clearest example?
options: The building of the Long Walls
The founding of the Delian League
The battle of Marathon
The expedition to Sicily
questions.explanation: Thucydides contrasts Pericles' warning not to extend the empire in wartime with the decision to invade Sicily in 415 BCE. The Long Walls, the League and Marathon all came before Pericles' death.

questions.stem: Comic poets such as Cratinus mocked Pericles' oddly shaped head, and Plutarch says sculptors showed him wearing a helmet. What should a historian conclude from comedy as a source on Pericles?
options: It is the most reliable source, since comic poets knew him personally
It is useless, since comedy never referred to living politicians
It records official decrees and so must be accepted as fact
It shows what audiences would laugh at, but exaggerates and distorts
questions.explanation: Old Comedy attacked leading men by name, so it reveals contemporary criticism and gossip about Pericles and Aspasia. Its jokes cannot be taken as fact without support from other sources.

questions.stem: In Plato's Gorgias, Socrates says he hears that Pericles made the Athenians lazy and greedy by introducing public pay. How should this view be weighed against Thucydides' praise?
options: It is a Spartan source and so is biased against all Athenians
It reflects a philosophical hostility to democracy, written after Pericles' death
It is an eyewitness record of Pericles' speeches in the assembly
It agrees fully with Thucydides, who also condemned public pay
questions.explanation: Plato wrote in the fourth century and was critical of democratic leaders, so his verdict shows a philosophical tradition rather than neutral assessment. Thucydides admired Pericles' judgement, so both views need context.

questions.stem: Thucydides knew Pericles and recorded his speeches, while Plutarch wrote his Life more than five centuries later. Which statement best compares them as sources?
options: Plutarch quotes only Pericles' own writings, so he needs no checking
Thucydides is closer to events, but his speeches are reconstructions shaped by his views
Plutarch is more reliable, because later writers always had access to better information
Thucydides is unreliable, because he never lived in Athens or saw Pericles
questions.explanation: Thucydides admits his speeches give the general sense of what was said in his own words, and he admired Pericles. Plutarch drew on earlier writers, including comic poets, and wrote to draw moral lessons from character.

questions.stem: Plutarch says Pericles left no writings apart from his decrees. Why does this matter for historians?
options: It shows that his speeches were all invented by later Romans
His words survive only as reported by others, such as Thucydides and Plutarch
It proves that Pericles could not read or write
It means none of his decrees were ever inscribed on stone
questions.explanation: Without his own writings, historians depend on other authors' versions of his speeches and policies, together with inscriptions and buildings. Each of these sources has its own purpose and limits.
